_what: The Green, a community green space on the street, built by tools/make-the-green.py: the view from the porch, the trail round the pond and every stop on it, the trailhead sign, the beds, and the screen under the porch roof with its rack. Ryan Boren's brief, 2026-10-05: next to the Truck Stop, a community green space with a covered porch, heavily wooded, with a wooden, accessible trail that goes in a meandering circle lined with beds of plants, flowers and vegetables you can eat, and a pond in the centre.
_light: It has just stopped raining. There is no sun, so nothing on the Green casts a shadow, and everything wet holds a line of the pale sky along its top edge: every leaf, every board, every rail. make-the-green.py refuses a shadow in the drawing and the vocabulary of sunshine in the room's voice.

trail._what: The boardwalk is built to the U.S. Access Board's standards for trails in outdoor developed areas, section 1017 of the Architectural Barriers Act standards, read 2026-10-05. The sign at the trailhead gives every figure 1017.10 asks a trailhead sign for, and make-the-green.py refuses a figure outside the standard.
trail.length: 1,100 feet, one loop, back to the porch
trail.surface: boards laid across the way you walk, with gaps no wider than half an inch, and a strip of grit on every board, because they are wet
trail.rest: a resting place at every stop, 60 inches long, beside the boards, with a bench that has a back and arms and room for a wheelchair beside it

_stops: Every stop on the loop, in the order you come to them from the porch. Each says what is there and what you might notice, in words, because the plan of the trail is aria-hidden; x and y are the stop's place on that plan, 600 by 400. Every plant is named by its common name only, the herbarium's rule: a Latin name typed from memory reads as a determination when it was a guess.

stops.name: The porch
stops.words: Where the trail starts and ends, under a roof, with the rain still running off its edge in a line of drops. The trailhead sign is on the post by the steps, and the steps have a ramp beside them as wide as they are.
stops.notice: The drip off the gutter, and the smell of the wet boards.

stops.name: The herb bed
plants: mint, in a pot of its own, because mint runs
stops.words: A raised bed at the first turn of the boardwalk, its rim at the height of a seat, planted with things that smell when you touch them.
stops.notice: Brush the rosemary and your hand smells of it for an hour. The lavender is heavy with water and bent over the rim.

stops.name: The vegetable beds
stops.words: Three long raised beds along the boardwalk, every one 27 inches high, the height the University of Minnesota's extension service gives as comfortable for gardening from a wheelchair. Everything in them was planted to be eaten, and anybody may pick what is ripe.
stops.notice: Wet tomato leaves, which smell green, and beads of water standing on the kale.

stops.name: The pond's edge
stops.words: A wide landing over the water, with a rail along the edge at the height of somebody sitting. The last of the rain is still putting rings on the pond, and there are lily pads at this end.
stops.notice: Frogs, now that it has stopped. The rings spreading and crossing each other.

stops.name: The bridge
stops.words: Where the boardwalk crosses the pond's outflow, a little stream that runs into the trees. The bridge rises one inch in every twenty on each side, the steepest the trail ever gets.
stops.notice: Water going over stones, louder than usual after the rain.

stops.name: The rain garden
stops.words: A shallow dip below the boardwalk where the water off the boards and the porch roof runs to, planted with things that like their feet wet. It is full now, and will be dry again by tomorrow.
stops.notice: Standing water with the sky in it, and the rushes bent over by the rain and straightening.

stops.name: The pollinator bed
stops.words: A long bed on the far side of the pond, planted for bees and butterflies. Nothing is flying yet: they wait for it to dry.
stops.notice: The coneflowers' heads full of water, and the bee balm bowed over under the rain it is still holding.

stops.name: The fern bed
stops.words: Where the boardwalk goes back in under the trees, a bed of things that grow in shade, and the softest things on the Green to touch.
stops.notice: Every leaf over you still dripping. The moss is cold and soaked through.

stops.name: The bench in the wood
stops.words: A bench with a back and arms, on a resting place beside the boards, with room beside it for a wheelchair. You can see the porch from here, and the pond through the trees.
stops.notice: The quiet, which is mostly the drip.

_quotes: Two quotations, both read on our own Nature page and checked against the Knowledge System mirror's copy of it word for word on every build when the mirror is there, and credited to the book they come from as read on that page: nobody read the books for this room. The Town Hall's rule: when our page changes, re-copy the quotation, never loosen the check.

quotes.words: A covered porch – allowing learning to stay outdoors in any weather – was essential.
quotes.who: Ira David Socol, Pam Moran and Chad Ratliff
quotes.about: writing about William Alcott's schools in the 1830s

quotes.words: petrichor, the delicious earthy scent after rainfall, when oil from plants is released into the air.
